claim: In the WSTS classification, Total Logic (L99) is made up of digital bipolar (L1), MOS general-purpose logic (L2a), MOS gate arrays (L2b), MOS standard cells and field-programmable logic (L2c), MOS display drivers (L3), MOS touch-screen controllers (L4) and MOS special-purpose logic (LA).
evidence: "L99 Total Logic. Total of items L1, L2a to L2c, L3, L4 and LA (L5 to L9)." and subcategory list "Digital Bipolar (code L1) MOS General Purpose Logic (code L2a) MOS Gate Arrays (code L2b) MOS Standard Cells and Field Programmable Logic (code L2c) MOS Display Drivers (code L3) MOS Touch Screen Controller (code L4) MOS Special Purpose Logic (code LA)" (WSTS Product Classification 2021, section 3.4.3)

claim: WSTS MOS special-purpose logic (LA) holds application-specific standard products (ASSPs) designed by the chip maker and customer-specific ICs (CSICs) designed by the customer, each designed for one application segment.
evidence: "LA. MOS Special Purpose Logic – The devices in this category are either (i) Application Specific Standard Products (ASSP) designed by semiconductor manufacturer or (ii) Customer Specific Integrated Circuits (CSIC) designed by the customer, all of which are specifically designed for one of the application segments listed below." (Product Classification 2021, p. 19)

claim: WSTS splits MOS special-purpose logic into five application segments: consumer (L5), computer and peripherals (L6), communication (L7), automotive (L8) and multipurpose and other (L9).
evidence: "MOS Special Purpose Logic (code LA) contains the following subcategories, i.e. Consumer (code L5), Computer and Peripherals (code L6), Communication (code L7), Automotive (code L8) and Multipurpose and Other (code L9)." (Product Classification 2021, p. 20)

claim: WSTS defines an ASSP as a chip whose design is controlled by the semiconductor maker to fill an application-specific need, listed in catalogues and sold to any customer.
evidence: "Application Specific Standard Products (ASSP) are designed or their design is controlled by the semiconductor manufacturer to fill an application specific need in a given market segment. The manufacturer lists the devices in catalogs and sells them to any customer." (Product Classification 2021, p. 19)

claim: WSTS counts a customer-specific IC (CSIC, 'full custom') under special-purpose logic only when its application is evident and sizeable; all other CSICs go to MOS gate arrays (L2b) or MOS standard cells (L2c).
evidence: "This category should only include those CSICs for which the application is obviously evident to semiconductor manufacturer and for which the application market is relatively sizable, such as ICs for watches. All other CSICs shall be classified in MOS Gate Arrays (code L2b) or MOS Standard Cells (code L2c)." (Product Classification 2021, p. 20)

claim: WSTS reports FPGAs, PLDs and PALs (field-programmable logic devices) in category L2c together with standard-cell CSICs, split by application.
evidence: "Some typical examples are Programmable Logic Devices (PLD), Programmable Array Logics (PAL) and Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGA)." under "L2c. MOS Standard Cells and Field Programmable Logic" (Product Classification 2021, pp. 18-19)

claim: WSTS MOS general-purpose logic (L2a) is standard commodity catalogue logic such as simple gates, flip-flops and registers, excluding programmable devices and ASICs.
evidence: "L2a. MOS General Purpose Logic - Devices in this classification are standard commodity catalog products, usually simple gates, flip-flop circuits and registers. ... Excluded are catalog products of any programmable device or any Special Purpose Application Specific (ASIC) device." (Product Classification 2021, p. 18)

claim: WSTS classifies smartphone and tablet application processors (integrating CPU, GPU, connectivity and codecs, with or without modem) as logic (L7f, wireless communication under special-purpose logic), not as micro ICs.
evidence: "L7f. Wireless Communication – Application Processor. ICs designed for low power applications, especially smartphones, tablets ... which integrate multiple components including central processing unit, graphic processing unit and connectivity ... Application Processors which also integrate a modem should be reported in this category L7f, too." (p. 21)

claim: Under WSTS rules, a maker-designed IC with multiple functional cores including an MPU, MCU or DSP core is reported as logic, not micro; only 'pure' or core-dominant MPU/MCU/DSP products are micro.
evidence: "ICs, designed by semiconductor manufacturer and having multiple functional cores including MPU-, MCU- or DSP-core, are NOT to be reported in this MOS Micro category, but to be reported under appropriate MOS Logic categories (code L)" (Product Classification 2021, p. 13)

claim: WSTS 'Total Application Specific ICs' (Q99) is not reported by members but computed by data-collection agents as the sum of application-specific analog, MCUs, DSPs, standard cells/FPLDs and special-purpose logic.
evidence: "Q99 Total Application Specific ICs – Total of items JA (JB to JF), P2 (P51, P52 and P6), P4, L2c (L2e to L2j), and LA (L5 to L9)" ... "Items in Q99 (i.e. Q1 to Q6) are NOT to be reported by member companies. They are mathematical aggregation of world totals" (pp. 24-25)

claim: WSTS splits analog ICs into general-purpose analog (J0: amplifiers/comparators, signal conversion, interface, power management) and application-specific analog (JA: consumer, computer, communications, automotive, industrial and others).
evidence: "This Analog category contains General Purpose Analog (code J0) and Application Specific Analog (code JA) subcategories. The General Purpose Analog category is sub-divided into specific functional subcategories of Amplifiers/Comparators (Signal Conditioning), Signal Conversion, Interface, and Power Management ICs." (p. 7); hierarchy table JB-JF (p. 3)

claim: WSTS assigns mixed-signal chips to digital or analog by chip area: an IC is analog if at least 50% of its die area is analog circuitry.
evidence: "J. Analog. Devices are classified as ANALOG if at least 50% of the total die area of the integrated circuit(s) in the device is occupied by ANALOG circuitry." (Product Classification 2021, section 3.4.1)

claim: WSTS counts image sensors (CCD and CMOS image sensors) and all optical sensors in optoelectronics, not in sensors and actuators.
evidence: "F5. Image Sensors ... F5a. CCD & Other Image Sensors ... F5b. CMOS Image Sensors" (section 3.2) and "NOTE: All optical sensors are to be reported in the appropriate category of Optoelectronics." (section 3.3)

claim: The WSTS 2021 classification includes solar cells in optoelectronics, under 'Other Optoelectronics' (F6).
evidence: "F6. Other Optoelectronics - All other optoelectronics devices not specifically listed above, including fiber optic components and solar cells." (Product Classification 2021, section 3.2)
notes: Answers the open question in CLM-0016: an earlier search for 'solar' reported no matches, but the text is present in F6.

claim: WSTS sensors and actuators (H99) cover temperature and other non-optical sensors, pressure sensors, acceleration and yaw-rate sensors, magnetic-field sensors, and actuators such as ink-jet nozzles, micro-mirrors, solid-state relays and SAW filters.
evidence: "H1 Temperature & Other Sensors ... H2 Pressure Sensors ... H3 Acceleration and Yaw Rate Sensors ... H4 Magnetic Field Sensors ... H6. Actuators ... This includes, but is not limited to, ink jet nozzles, micro mirrors, solid-state relays, and SAW filters." (section 3.3)

claim: WSTS counts IGBTs, IGBT modules and MOSFET power transistors (power dissipation of 1W or more) as discrete power transistors, with separate value and unit reporting for bipolar/other, IGBT and MOSFET power-transistor groups.
evidence: "C9. Insulated Gate Bipolar Transistors (IGBT) ... C10. Insulated Gate Bipolar Transistor (IGBT) Modules" ... "the Total Worldwide Units shall be reported for each of the three product groups. CA. Bipolar and Other Power Transistors ... CC. MOSFET Power Transistors" (section 3.1, pp. 5-6)

claim: The WSTS 2021 classification has no separate product category for silicon-carbide or gallium-nitride devices: product classes are defined by function (e.g. power transistor, rectifier), and silicon carbide appears only as an example semiconductor material.
evidence: Searched the full text for 'silicon carbide', 'SiC', 'GaN', 'gallium': the only hit is the material list "Germanium, silicon, III V compounds such as gallium arsenide or polycrystalline materials such as selenium, silicon carbide..." (section 2); power categories C1-C10 are defined by device type and power rating.
notes: Based on the 2021 edition; newer editions (2023+) are behind SIA subscriber login.

claim: The 2021 WSTS classification has no explicit categories for HBM, data-center GPUs or AI accelerators: 'graphic processing unit' appears only inside the smartphone application-processor definition, and memory is split only into DRAM, SRAM, mask ROM/EPROM, flash and other memory.
evidence: Text search of Product Classification 2021: no match for 'HBM' or 'stack'; 'graphic processing unit' occurs only in L7f; "MOS Memory contains the following subcategories; DRAM (M1) SRAM (M2) Mask Programmable ROM & EPROM (M8) Flash Memory (M7) Other Memory (M6)" (section 3.4.4)

claim: WSTS states that the logic category's 2025 growth was driven by high-performance chips for data centers and AI accelerators, which places AI accelerators within WSTS logic.
evidence: "Logic devices delivered the largest contribution to overall market expansion, supported by demand for high-performance chips used in data centers, AI accelerators, and advanced computing systems." (WSTS full-year 2025 release, Product Segments)

claim: WSTS counts memory units at device level: a memory module is counted as its number of component chips, and partially good memories are prorated by the share of functional bits.
evidence: "For example: A company makes a DRAM module containing nine 128M DRAM devices. (section 3.4.4)

claim: TSMC's HPC share (58% for 2025, 66% in 2Q26) is far above WSTS's 45.5% computer end-use share for 2025. The measures differ: TSMC classifies its own foundry revenue by customer platform, which excludes memory and most analog/discretes, whereas WSTS counts all chip sales by final equipment.
notes: Compares CLM-0071 (TSMC 2025 platform split), @tsmc_plat and @eu25_comp. Also, TSMC's 'smartphone' maps to WSTS 'communications' (28.7% in 2025) and its 'automotive' (4-5%) is far below WSTS automotive (10.9%), consistent with automotive chips being mostly mature-node analog/discrete/MCU made outside TSMC's leading edge.

claim: Mapping across publishers: AI accelerators, custom data-center ASICs, smartphone application processors, FPGAs and display drivers all fall in WSTS 'logic'. CPUs are WSTS 'micro' (MPU) but 'advanced logic' for SIA and 'logic' for the OECD. HBM sits in memory (DRAM) everywhere. CMOS image sensors are WSTS optoelectronics. SiC/GaN power devices have no separate WSTS class.
notes: Built from @tx_la_def, @tx_fpga, @tx_ap, @tx_ai_logic, @tx_cis, @tx_wbg, @tx_hbm_gpu, @oecd_logic, @sia_adv_logic, CLM-0056 (Gartner counts HBM within DRAM).

claim: Worldwide semiconductor unit shipments for 2022-2025 from WSTS could not be found in public sources; SIA's annual releases stopped reporting units after 2021.
evidence: Searched SIA annual sales releases for 2022 (SRC-0108), 2023 (SRC-0055), 2024 (SRC-0054) and 2025 (SRC-0007): none mention units shipped; WSTS forecast releases (SRC-0001-0003) give US$ only; the WSTS unit data (241 categories, CLM-0003) are subscriber-only. The only 2025 unit figure found is Deloitte's estimate (1.05 trillion).

claim: Public revenue figures for WSTS sub-classes (ASSP vs CSIC within special-purpose logic, general-purpose logic, gate arrays, FPGAs/standard cells, display drivers, DRAM vs NAND, power management, image sensors) for 2020-2025 could not be found.
evidence: Searched WSTS forecast releases, SIA annual releases and SIA Factbooks 2022-2025: product detail stops at logic, memory, analog, MPU, MCU, DSP, opto, discretes and sensors. The only sub-class figures found are DRAM growth (+82.6% in 2024, SIA) and automotive ICs. Detail is in the subscriber-only Blue Book (57 categories, CLM-1257).

claim: End-market splits by units (rather than value), and end-use shares for 2019 and earlier, could not be found in public sources.
evidence: The SIA End Use Survey page describes a dollar-based survey (US$350, not in subscription); SIA SOI 2021-2026 and Factbooks 2022-2025 give dollar shares only, earliest 2020; no unit-based end-use data were found.
